a.raw: the prince stumbled through the dark tangled undergrowth
a.fixed: The prince stumbled through the dark, tangled undergrowth.
a.why: The starts the sentence, so it gets a capital T. Dark and tangled both describe the undergrowth, so a comma goes between them. A period ends it.

b.raw: jemmy pushed through the thick thorny brambles
b.fixed: Jemmy pushed through the thick, thorny brambles.
b.why: Jemmy starts the sentence and is a name, so it gets a capital J. Thick and thorny both describe the brambles, so a comma goes between them. A period ends it.

items.title: Where, when, or how?
items.q: Jemmy ran through the tangle. What does through the tangle tell you?
items.why: The tangle is a place in the forest. It tells where.

miss.1: Is the tangle a time? It is a place.
miss.2: It is not the way he ran. It is a place.

items.title: How many?
items.q: How many prepositions? Betsy came from the woods with a coil of rope.
items.why: From the woods, with a coil, of rope: three.

miss.0: Look again. Find from, with, and one more small word.
miss.1: Look again. There is one more small word after coil.

items.title: Find the preposition
items.q: Which word is the preposition? The prince followed Jemmy into the brambles.
items.why: Into sits in front of the brambles and tells where.

miss.0: Followed is what the prince did. Look for the small word in front of the brambles.
miss.2: Brambles is a noun. Look for the small word in front of it.

items.title: Where, when, or how?
items.q: The soldiers rode along the river road. What does it tell you?
items.why: The river road is a place. It tells where.

miss.1: Is the river road a time? It is a place.
miss.2: It is not the way they rode. It is a place.

items.title: The root spect
items.q: A prospector searches rivers and hills for gold. Which part of the word tells you he looks?
items.why: Spect means look. A prospector looks for gold.

miss.0: Pro is at the front. Find the root that means look.
miss.2: Or means a person who. Find the root that means look.

items.title: Soft or hard?
items.q: Say cent. Is the c soft or hard?
items.why: The next letter is e, so the c is soft. Cent sounds like sent.

miss.1: Look at the letter after the c. It is e.

items.title: Soft or hard?
items.q: Say goose. Is the g soft or hard?
items.why: The next letter is o, so the g stays hard.

miss.0: Look at the letter after the g. It is o, not e, i, or y.
Clap it: for, est. Two beats.
miss.2: Clap it: out, law. Two beats.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back, it’s Opti. The prince just gave away Jemmy’s hiding place. Now Jemmy has one chance, and he takes it. Today there’s a chase, a big surprise in a clearing, and an argument. As you read, ask yourself: does the prince have a point?
transcripts.guide1: Word study. You’ll match more words with the root that means look, and you’ll hunt for prepositions. Most sentences have more than one. There’s a bonus too: c and g can make two different sounds.
transcripts.guide2: Before you read: Chapter 13 moves fast, so hang on. After the chase, the boys argue. Listen to both sides. Then in Chapter 14, a girl comes through the woods calling for someone named Petunia.
transcripts.guide3: A strong ending gives your reader something to think about. Today, try ending with a question, or a challenge. Make it sound finished.

notes.wordParts: The root spect means “look.” inspect = look closely into, spectator = one who looks on, respect = look again with care, inspector = one whose job is to look.
notes.grammar: A preposition sits in front of a noun and ties it to the sentence. It can tell where (under the straw), when (after the storm), or how (with great care).
notes.spelling: To read a long word, split it into beats: im·por·tant. The letters c and g go soft before e, i, or y: city, giant. Before other letters they stay hard: cave, goat.
notes.wgrd: Good readers notice what characters say and how they say it. When two characters argue, each one may have a point.
vocab: a natural way of acting without stopping to think
at full tilt means as fast as you can go

mods.script: Here's a short poem about a little turtle. Is it a haiku? Let's check. A haiku has three lines: five beats, then seven, then five. And a haiku doesn't rhyme. Read the turtle poem out loud. Count the lines. Then listen to the ends of the lines. Do any of them rhyme? Now give two reasons it is not a haiku.

mods.script: Here's a bonus. Say these two words: cat, and city. Both start with c. But they don't sound the same! The letter after the c is the clue. When c or g comes right before e, i, or y, it goes soft. C says s, and g says j. Before any other letter, they stay hard. Say the eight words in the sort, and think about the questions. Think about this before you read. The prince gave Jemmy away. Then, after the chase, the prince says, Then I forgive you. Forgive Jemmy? For what? Watch both boys while they argue. Each one thinks he is the one who got wronged.

In Chapter 14, a girl comes through the woods calling for someone named Petunia. Then watch my video in the Read Like a Writer box before you try it.

mods.label: Opti shows you how
mods.script: [warmly] Read Like a Writer has three parts. Let me show you with a different sentence, from Chapter 14. Brambles, reaching out like cat's claws, tore at their fine garments. Part one, read like a reader. What is happening? The boys push through thorny bushes, and the thorns rip their fancy clothes. Part two, read like a writer. What does the author do? He says the brambles are like cat's claws, so we can almost feel the scratch. Part three, mimic. Here's mine: The snow, stinging like tiny bees, bit at my cheeks. Now it's your turn with the chase sentence. Write one sentence in each box.

mods.todo: Pick Explorer or Scholar. Answer the three questions in full sentences.
mods.script: Now answer in full sentences, with details from the book. One, tell Jemmy's escape step by step: how he gets out of the hut, what he does in the forest, and where he hides. Two, what does the prince say when Jemmy says, You betrayed me? Three, who is Betsy looking for, and which way does she point? For a challenge, pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.

mods.todo: Write your conclusion again. End with a question or a challenge.
mods.script: Endings matter. Listen to Clara's first conclusion. It's fine, but it doesn't make you think. Her new one ends with a question: if no one ever teaches a prince to care about others, what kind of king will he become? Now that's an ending! Write your conclusion again. End with a question, or a challenge that starts with, If he never learns.

cards.instinct: Instinct. A thoroughbred of the streets, Jemmy acted on instinct. Instinct is doing something without stopping to think.
cards.foliage: Foliage. Jemmy turned to the right and beat his way back into the foliage. Foliage means the leaves and branches of plants.
cards.tilt: Tilt. Jemmy covered the ground at full tilt. At full tilt means as fast as you can go.
cards.bramble: Bramble. Brambles, reaching out like cat's claws, tore at their fine garments. A bramble is a prickly, thorny bush.

virtue.name: courage
virtue.title: Courage Watch: Did they show courage?

items.t: Jemmy bursts out of the straw and runs for the door before Cutwater can grab him.
items.why: He moves fast, even with an outlaw right there.

items.t: The prince tells Jemmy, “Then I forgive you,” when it was the prince who gave Jemmy away.
items.why: Forgiving someone for being angry with you is not courage.

items.t: Jemmy steps out of the trees and asks Betsy, a stranger, which way to the river.
items.why: He doesn’t know who she is, but he speaks up to get help.
